newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Official urges Israel prepare for Syria war.
newsitem.headline: Official urges Israel prepare for Syria war.

text.p: Former Soviet Jewish dissident Natan Sharansky, now Israel's minister of trade and industry, urged the government to prepare the public for war with Syria in an interview published on Sunday.

"In light of the Syrian threats, and they are very serious in my opinion, the best way is to begin preparing the people for the possiblity of war," Sharansky told Israel's daily Haaretz in an interview.
Syrian troop movements in Lebanon last month and a series of military exercises have given Israel war jitters. Damascus has said the redeployment was defensive.
"Instead of all the time saying that it is not serious -- and I'm not saying that the government says that -- we have to have a public information campaign, discussions in the schools."
Later on Sunday, in a news conference at Israel's border with Lebanon, Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai reiterated Israel would remain prepared but hoped for calm.

"We have an interest in calm. We have no aims across the border. We are taking preparedness and alertness steps. I appeal to (Syrian President Hafez al-) Assad and the Syrians to return to the negotiating table," Mordechai said.

Sharansky, whose new Yisrael ba-Aliya party garnered seven seats in Israel's 120-seat parliament in Israel's May elections, admitted he was not well-versed in Middle East culture but said life in the Soviet Union helped him to understand Syria.

"I do not know the Arab mentality," Sharansky said. "But I know the totalitarian regime well. Its stability is conditioned on the existence of enemies. Therefore they have to threaten and if someone is weak they go further. That's how it was in Russia."

Sharansky, 48, spent nine years in Soviet prisons before winning his freedom in an East-West swap in 1986. He came to Israel as a hero. His party draws support from more than half a million Jews from the former Soviet Union who have immigrated to Israel since the late 1980s.
The minister said he believed there could be no peace talks with Damascus until it liberalised its regime.

"There has to be a process of internal opening in Syria, that would start with the possibility of hearing other voices and end with a change in the study plan in the schools. In parallel, I would be willing to build negotiations based on concessions," Sharansky said.

More than five years of peace talks between Israel and Syria have stalled over the Golan Heights captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war. Damascus demands a full Israeli withdrawal. The previous government was prepared to make at least a partial withdrawal.
Right-wing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who ousted the centre-left government in the May elections, has vowed never to give up the strategic plateau.
